The Mars Exploration Rover (MER) Opportunity is one of two identical spacecraft launched in 2003 and sent to different landing sites on Mars. The Athena Science Payload on the rover enabled advanced analysis of Martian soil and rocks, with instruments mounted on a robotic arm and a panoramic camera for imaging. The spacecraft's design drew from the Mars Pathfinder Sojourner rover and included a complex entry, descent, and landing system utilizing a backshell, heat shield, and parachute. The rover was equipped with a sophisticated mobility system allowing it to traverse various terrains and was powered by solar panels and rechargeable batteries.

pds:Internal_Reference.pds:comment: The Tracking Data File (TDF, or sometimes Archival Tracking Data File -- ATDF) is produced by JPL multi-mission support personnel for use in determining spacecraft trajectories, gravity fields affecting them and radio propagation conditions. The typical TDF has a single File Identification Logical Record (Table), one Transponder Logical Record (Table), a Tracking Data Table of many records, and one or more padding records to fill out a data block. Some TDFs may be missing the Identification, Transponder, and/or padding records. Each TDF logical record contains 288 bytes; 28 logical records are packed into each block of 8064 bytes. Each TDF is an integer number of these blocks. Tracking Data Table format and content are described by JPL/DSN Document 820-13, TRK-2-25 (various effective dates, with significant changes in 1997). The applicable version for this archive is dated December 15, 1998.

pds:Field_Bit.pds:description: Item 1: Record Format for the File Identification Logical Record (set to 8).
Item 2: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 3: The Record Type (set to 10).
Item 4: The year in which the file was created, modulo 1900.
Item 5: The day-of-year in which the file was created.
Item 6: The hour in which the file was created.
Item 7: The minute in which the file was created.
Item 8: The second in which the file was created.
Item 9: Reserved bits (set to 0).

Item 10: ID number for the spacecraft. These are specified in DSN document OPS-6-8. Representative values include Magellan 18 Voyager 1 31 Voyager 2 32 Clementine 64 Galileo Orbiter 77 Cassini 82 Mars Global Surveyor 94.
Item 11: First of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 82 (='R').
Item 12: Second of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 47 (='/').
Item 13: Third of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 84 (='T').
Item 14: Fourth of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 32 (='').
Item 15: Fifth of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 65 (='A').
Item 16: Sixth of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 84 (='T').
Item 17: Seventh of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 68 (='D').
Item 18: Eighth of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 70 (='F').
Item 19: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 20: Four unused bits (set to 0).
Item 1: The Record Format for the Transponder Logical Record (set to 8).
Item 2: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 3: Record Type of the Transponder Logical Record (set to 30).
Item 4: The year in which the transponder was turned on, modulo 1900.
Item 5: The day-of-year in which the transponder was turned on.
Item 6: The hour in which the transponder was turned on.
Item 7: The minute in which the transponder was turned on.
Item 8: The second in which the transponder was turned on.
Item 9: Reserved bits (set to 0).

Item 10: ID number for the spacecraft. These are specified in DSN document OPS-6-8. Representative values include Magellan 18 Voyager 1 31 Voyager 2 32 Clementine 64 Galileo Orbiter 77 Cassini 82 Mars Global Surveyor 94.
Item 11: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 12: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 13: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 14: The year in which the transponder was turned off, modulo 1900.
Item 15: The day-of-year in which the transponder was turned off.
Item 16: The hour in which the transponder was turned off.
Item 17: The minute in which the transponder was turned off.
Item 18: The second in which the transponder was turned off.
Item 19: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 20: Four high-order bits in archaic implementations that used 36-bit words; no longer needed, and now set to 0.
Item 21: The high part (HP) of the spacecraft transponder frequency. The value is positive and less than 2^24.
Item 22: Four high-order bits in archaic implementations that used 36-bit words; no longer used, and is now set to 0.

Item 23: The low part (LP) of the spacecraft transponder frequency. This value is positive and less than 2^24. The true spacecraft transponder frequency (in Hertz) can be recovered by calculating HP*10^4 + LP*10^-3.
Item 24: Unused bits (set to 0).

Item 1: A 32-bit code which identifies the format of the Tracking Data Logical Records (TDLRs); set to: 8 for records defined by SFOC-NAV-2-25 (1997-04-15 and after) 4 for records defined by TRK-2-25 (1997-04-14 and before). This definition of TDLR format is INCORRECT if Record Format = 4.
Item 2: Not used under SFOC-NAV-2-25; set to 0.
Item 3: The type of data in the TDLRs; set to: 90 for low-rate data 91 for high-rate data
Item 4: The year modulo 1900 in the TDLR time tag.
Item 5: The day of year in the TDLR time tag.
Item 6: The hour in the TDLR time tag.
Item 7: The minute in the TDLR time tag.
Item 8: The second in the TDLR time tag.
Item 9: Not used under SFOC-NAV-2-25; set to 0.
Item 10: The ID number of the receiving station DSN antenna.
Item 11: Receiver/downlink frequency band. 0 N/A or Ku-Band 1 S-Band 2 X-Band 3 Ka-Band.

Item 12: dentifier for the data type in the TDLR. 1 High-Rate Doppler 2 Low-Rate Doppler 3 Uplink Phase 4 DRVID 5 Range 6 Ramp 7 Mixed 8 Allan Deviation (if Item 119 = 0,1,2) or Smoothed Noise (if Item 119 = 3) 11 High-Rate Downlink Phase 12 Low-Rate Downlink Phase DSN definition of Smoothed Noise: Noise of the Metric Data Assembly (MDA) Doppler Pseudo-Residuals smoothed over six different sample periods: 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 200, and 600 seconds. These items are the standard deviation of the data after linearly detrending using a least squares fit. Data for each interval are smoothed over that time interval, noise is computed on 18 samples, and each result is divided by 0.99534520 to account for filter loss at high frequencies because of the linear fit.
Item 13: Doppler channel count.

Item 14: Data collection mode on the ground. 0 Angles or Ramp or Uplink Phase 1 1-way, Doppler or Mixed 2 2-way, Doppler or Mixed 3 3-way, Doppler or Mixed 4 3-way Coherent, Doppler, or Mixed 5 1-way, Range or DRVID or Allan Deviation or Smoothed Noise 6 2-way, Range or DRVID or Allan Deviation or Smoothed Noise 7 3-way, Range or DRVID or Allan Deviation or Smoothed Noise.

Item 15: ID number for the spacecraft. These are specified in DSN document OPS-6-8. Representative values include Magellan 18 Voyager 1 31 Voyager 2 32 Clementine 64 Galileo Orbiter 77 Cassini 82 Mars Global Surveyor 94 Dawn 203 MESSENGER 236.
Item 16: The type of range data collected 0 No Range Data 1 GSTDN (RE) 6 PLOP or Pseudo-Noise (PRA) 7 PLOP2 (SRA) 8 MU2.
Item 17: The type of range data collected 0 No Angle Data 1 Azimuth/Elevation 2 Hour Angle/Declination 3 X/Y (where +X is East) 4 X/Y (where +X is South).
Item 18: The type of DRVID data collected 0 No DRVID Data 6-8 Same as for Range Type (Item 16).
Item 19: Quality of Doppler measurement.
Item 20: Doppler Bias.
Item 21: Quality of angle measurements.
Item 22: Reference for frequency estimates 0 DCO Level (22 MHz) 1 Sky Level.
Item 23: Simulation Synthesizer Indicator.
Item 24: Receiver Loop Lock Indicator.
Item 25: Transmitter On/Off Indicator.
Item 26: Doppler reference receiver type: 2 MFR 3 Block III 4 Block IV 5 Block V 6 DGT, (arrayed or single station) 7 FSR, arrayed
Item 27: Source designation/exciter type: 1 34-m or 70-m Subnet, Block III/IV Exciter 2 26-m Subnet 3 11-m (OVLBI, Orbiting VLBI) Subnet 4 34-m or 70-m Subnet, Block V Exciter.
Item 28: No process flag and cause: 1 before AOS/after LOS 2 'frozen' Doppler counter 3 illegal reference frequency.
Item 29: Sample Interval in hundredths of a second.
Item 30: High part of Doppler count or downlink phase. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 31: Intermediate part of Doppler count or downlink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 30. Unit is count.
Item 32: Low part of Doppler count or downlink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 30. Unit is count.

Item 33: High part of Range. To reconstruct the double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6. Unit of the reconstructed value is nanosecond (ns) if Range Type (Item 16) is 1; otherwise, unit is Range-Unit (RU). A Range-Unit is approximately one nanosecond; it is defined as a function of the sky frequency in Hertz (f_sky) and the uplink frequency band: RU(sec) = 0.5*10^-18*f_sky (S-Band uplink) = (11/75)*10^-18*f_sky (HEF X-Band uplink) = (221/1498)*10^-18*f_sky (Block-V Exciter X-Band uplink).
Item 34: Intermediate part of Range. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 33.
Item 35: Low part of Range. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 33.
Item 36: Lowest (last) ranging component.
Item 37: Part 1 of uplink phase. To reconstruct quadruple precision value from four parts, use: (Part 1)*2^40 + (Part 2)*2^16 + (Part 3)*2^-8 + (Part 4)*2^-32 Unit is cycle.
Item 38: Part 2 of uplink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 37.
Item 39: Part 3 of uplink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 37.
Item 40: Part 4 of uplink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 37.
Item 41: Depending on Angle Type (Item 17) the azimuth, hour angle, or X value for the antenna. Unit is millidegree.
Item 42: Depending on Angle Type (Item 17) the azimuth, hour angle, or Y value for the antenna. Unit is millidegree.

Item 43: If Item 22 is 0, the high part of the Doppler reference frequency (DCO is near 22 MHz). If Item 22 is 1, the sky frequency for the receiver (S-Band near 2 GHz, X-Band near 7 GHz, Ku-Band near 15 GHz, Ka-Band near 32 GHz). The double precision value (in Hertz) can be reconstructed using (HP)*10^3 + (LP)*10^-6.

Item 44: Depending on Frequency Level Indicator (Item 22) the low part of the Doppler reference or the receiver frequency. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 43.
Item 45: Differential range versus integrated Doppler (DRVID) in hundredths of a Range-Unit.

Item 46: High part of the second high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 47: Intermediate part of the second high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 46. Unit is count.

Item 48: Depending on the Sample Data Type ID (Item 12) this can be (1) the low part of the second high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement; (2) round trip light time (operator input to ranging system; unit is second); (3) 0.1-second Allan Deviation (unit is dimensionless 10^-17); or (4) 0.1-second Smoothed Noise (unit is dimensionless 10^-6).

Item 49: High part of the third high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 50: Intermediate part of the third high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 49. Unit is count.

Item 51: Depending on the Sample Data Type ID (Item 12) this can be (1) the low part of the third high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement; (2) time at which the integration of the last ranging frequency component is completed (a round number, not used for analysis; unit is second); (3) 1-second Allan Deviation (unit is dimensionless 10^-17); or (4) 1-second Smoothed Noise (unit is dimensionless 10^-6).

Item 52: High part of the fourth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 53: Intermediate part of the fourth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 52. Unit is count.

Item 54: Depending on the Sample Data Type ID (Item 12) this can be (1) the low part of the fourth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement; (2) T1 integration time constant (unit is second); (3) 10-second Allan Deviation (unit is dimensionless 10^-17); or (4) 10-second Smoothed Noise (unit is dimensionless 10^-6).

Item 55: High part of the fifth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 56: Intermediate part of the fifth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 55. Unit is count.

Item 57: Depending on the Sample Data Type ID (Item 12) this can be (1) the low part of the fifth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement; (2) T2 integration time constant (unit is second); (3) 100-second Allan Deviation (unit is dimensionless 10^-17); or (4) 100-second Smoothed Noise (unit is dimensionless 10^-6).

Item 58: High part of the sixth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 59: Intermediate part of the sixth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 58. Unit is count.

Item 60: Depending on the Sample Data Type ID (Item 12) this can be (1) the low part of the sixth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement; (2) T3 integration time constant (unit is second); (3) 1000-second Allan Deviation (unit is dimensionless 10^-17); or (4) 200-second Smoothed Noise (unit is dimensionless 10^-6).

Item 61: High part of the seventh high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 62: Intermediate part of the seventh high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 61. Unit is count.

Item 63: Depending on the Sample Data Type ID (Item 12) this can be (1) the low part of the seventh high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement; (2) Reference (0-degree) Correlation Voltage (in millivolts); or (3) 600-second Smoothed Noise (unit is dimensionless 10^-6).

Item 64: High part of the eighth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 65: Intermediate part of the eighth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 64. Unit is count.

Item 66: Depending on the Sample Data Type ID (Item 12) this can be (1) the low part of the eighth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement; (2) Quadrature (90-degree) Correlation Voltage (in millivolts).

Item 67: High part of the ninth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 68: Intermediate part of the ninth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 67. Unit is count.
Item 68: Low part of the ninth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 67. Unit is count.

Item 70: High part of the tenth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 71: Intermediate part of the tenth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 70. Unit is count.
Item 72: Low part of the tenth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 70. Unit is count.
Item 73: Sign bits/extension for Item 74; an artifact of 36-bit binary definitions in older formats. The full value (including sign) is captured in Item 74.
Item 74: Doppler pseudo-residual in millihertz.
Item 75: Sign bits/extension for Item 76; an artifact of 36-bit binary definitions in older formats. The full value (including sign) is captured in Item 76.
Item 76: Range pseudo-residual. Unit is 10^-3 nanosecond if Range Type (Item 16) is set to 1; unit is milli-Range-Unit for other types of range data.
Item 77: Angle 1 pseudo-residual (see Item 41) in millidegree, or numerator for spacecraft turnaround ratio.
Item 78: Angle 1 pseudo-residual (see Item 42) in millidegree, or denominator for spacecraft turnaround ratio.
Item 79: Exciter/Uplink Frequency Band. Allowable values include: 0 N/A, or Ku-Band; S-Band in TRK-2-14 1 S-Band 2 X-Band 3 Ka-Band 7 S-Band in TRK-2-20.
Item 80: Control mode for antenna tracking. Allowable values include: 0 Auto Track 1 Manual Aided 2 Computer 3 Sidereal 4 Brake
Item 81: Conscan mode for antenna tracking. Allowable values include: 0 Conscan OFF 1 Closed Loop 2 Open Loop.
Item 82: Angle 1 (Item 77) Pseudo-Residual tolerance.
Item 83: Angle 2 (Item 78) Pseudo-Residual tolerance.
Item 84: Doppler (Item 74) Pseudo-Residual tolerance.
Item 85: Doppler noise tolerance.
Item 86: Percentage of data used for Allan Deviation calculation (e.g., Items 48, 51, etc.), or ranging equipment delay (item 104) Overflow in hundredths of a Range-Unit.
Item 87: Total Slipped Cycles during Doppler Count.

Item 89: Received Signal Strength in hundredths of dBm (deciBel referenced to one milliwatt).
Item 90: Exciter station delay in nanosecond.

Item 92: Range modulation On/Off state.

Item 105: Range or DRVID Power-to-Noise Ratio in tenths of a dB.
Item 106: Sign bits/extension for Item 107; an artifact of 36-bit binary definitions in older formats.
Item 107: Average Doppler Pseudo-Residual (in milliHertz) or Orbiting Very Long Baseline Interferometer (OVLBI) Train Axis Angle (in millidegrees).
Item 108: Sign bits/extension for Item 109; an artifact of 36-bit binary definitions in older formats.

Item 109: If Item 12 is a Doppler data type, the intermediate part (IP) of Delta Frequency divided by Frequency (in dimensionless units of 10^-14); the double precision value can be recovered from (IP)*10^-7 + (LP)*10^-14 If Item 12 indicates range data, the Pseudo DRVID (in units of hundredths of a Range-Unit).
Item 110: Sign bits/extension for Item 111; an artifact of 36-bit binary definitions in older formats. Set to zero.

Item 119: If Item 12 is 6, the Ramp Controller Indicator (RCI); allowable values are: 0 POCA 1 DCO 2 Block V Exciter If Item 12 is 8 and this Item is 0, 1, or 2, the Cause of Allan Deviation Report Generation (ADRG); allowable values are: 0 1000-second report 1 Doppler mode change 2 IDLE mode If Item 12 is 8 and this Item is 3, the data type is radio science smoothed noise.

Raw radio tracking data
The external_source_product_identifier is formed from the PDS3 DATA_SET_ID, an ASCII colon character, and the PDS3 data object file name.

The File Identification Table identifies the type of data, the spacecraft, and the date and time at which the file was created It is made up of one File Identification Record. On some ATDFs, the File Identification Table may be omitted. When present, it is the first record in the file.
The contents of the File Identification Record packed into 31 bytes. The final 257 bytes of the record are not used and their contents are set to 0.
Item 1: Record Format for the File Identification Logical Record (set to 8).
Item 2: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 3: The Record Type (set to 10).
Item 4: The year in which the file was created, modulo 1900.
Item 5: The day-of-year in which the file was created.
Item 6: The hour in which the file was created.
Item 7: The minute in which the file was created.
Item 8: The second in which the file was created.
Item 9: Reserved bits (set to 0).

Item 10: ID number for the spacecraft. These are specified in DSN document OPS-6-8. Representative values include Magellan 18 Voyager 1 31 Voyager 2 32 Clementine 64 Galileo Orbiter 77 Cassini 82 Mars Global Surveyor 94.
Item 11: First of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 82 (='R').
Item 12: Second of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 47 (='/').
Item 13: Third of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 84 (='T').
Item 14: Fourth of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 32 (='').
Item 15: Fifth of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 65 (='A').
Item 16: Sixth of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 84 (='T').
Item 17: Seventh of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 68 (='D').
Item 18: Eighth of eight character codes identifying the type of data contained in the file. Set to 70 (='F').
Item 19: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 20: Four unused bits (set to 0).

The Transponder Table identifies the spacecraft, the date and time when the transponder went ON, the date and time when the transponder went OFF, and the spacecraft transponder frequency. It is made up of one Transponder Logical Record. The Transponder table may be omitted from the ATDF; when present, there is only one Transponder Logical Record and it is usually the second record in the ATDF.
The items of the ATDF File Transponder Logical Record Group.
Item 1: The Record Format for the Transponder Logical Record (set to 8).
Item 2: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 3: Record Type of the Transponder Logical Record (set to 30).
Item 4: The year in which the transponder was turned on, modulo 1900.
Item 5: The day-of-year in which the transponder was turned on.
Item 6: The hour in which the transponder was turned on.
Item 7: The minute in which the transponder was turned on.
Item 8: The second in which the transponder was turned on.
Item 9: Reserved bits (set to 0).

Item 10: ID number for the spacecraft. These are specified in DSN document OPS-6-8. Representative values include Magellan 18 Voyager 1 31 Voyager 2 32 Clementine 64 Galileo Orbiter 77 Cassini 82 Mars Global Surveyor 94.
Item 11: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 12: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 13: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 14: The year in which the transponder was turned off, modulo 1900.
Item 15: The day-of-year in which the transponder was turned off.
Item 16: The hour in which the transponder was turned off.
Item 17: The minute in which the transponder was turned off.
Item 18: The second in which the transponder was turned off.
Item 19: Reserved bits (set to 0).
Item 20: Four high-order bits in archaic implementations that used 36-bit words; no longer needed, and now set to 0.
Item 21: The high part (HP) of the spacecraft transponder frequency. The value is positive and less than 2^24.
Item 22: Four high-order bits in archaic implementations that used 36-bit words; no longer used, and is now set to 0.

Item 23: The low part (LP) of the spacecraft transponder frequency. This value is positive and less than 2^24. The true spacecraft transponder frequency (in Hertz) can be recovered by calculating HP*10^4 + LP*10^-3.
Item 24: Unused bits (set to 0).
The Tracking Data Table contains the spacecraft tracking data. It is made up of one or more Tracking Data Logical Records (TDLRs).
Contents of the Tracking Data Logical Record.

Item 1: A 32-bit code which identifies the format of the Tracking Data Logical Records (TDLRs); set to: 8 for records defined by SFOC-NAV-2-25 (1997-04-15 and after) 4 for records defined by TRK-2-25 (1997-04-14 and before). This definition of TDLR format is INCORRECT if Record Format = 4.
Item 2: Not used under SFOC-NAV-2-25; set to 0.
Item 3: The type of data in the TDLRs; set to: 90 for low-rate data 91 for high-rate data
Item 4: The year modulo 1900 in the TDLR time tag.
Item 5: The day of year in the TDLR time tag.
Item 6: The hour in the TDLR time tag.
Item 7: The minute in the TDLR time tag.
Item 8: The second in the TDLR time tag.
Item 9: Not used under SFOC-NAV-2-25; set to 0.
Item 10: The ID number of the receiving station DSN antenna.
Item 11: Receiver/downlink frequency band. 0 N/A or Ku-Band 1 S-Band 2 X-Band 3 Ka-Band.

Item 12: dentifier for the data type in the TDLR. 1 High-Rate Doppler 2 Low-Rate Doppler 3 Uplink Phase 4 DRVID 5 Range 6 Ramp 7 Mixed 8 Allan Deviation (if Item 119 = 0,1,2) or Smoothed Noise (if Item 119 = 3) 11 High-Rate Downlink Phase 12 Low-Rate Downlink Phase DSN definition of Smoothed Noise: Noise of the Metric Data Assembly (MDA) Doppler Pseudo-Residuals smoothed over six different sample periods: 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 200, and 600 seconds. These items are the standard deviation of the data after linearly detrending using a least squares fit. Data for each interval are smoothed over that time interval, noise is computed on 18 samples, and each result is divided by 0.99534520 to account for filter loss at high frequencies because of the linear fit.
Item 13: Doppler channel count.

Item 14: Data collection mode on the ground. 0 Angles or Ramp or Uplink Phase 1 1-way, Doppler or Mixed 2 2-way, Doppler or Mixed 3 3-way, Doppler or Mixed 4 3-way Coherent, Doppler, or Mixed 5 1-way, Range or DRVID or Allan Deviation or Smoothed Noise 6 2-way, Range or DRVID or Allan Deviation or Smoothed Noise 7 3-way, Range or DRVID or Allan Deviation or Smoothed Noise.

Item 15: ID number for the spacecraft. These are specified in DSN document OPS-6-8. Representative values include Magellan 18 Voyager 1 31 Voyager 2 32 Clementine 64 Galileo Orbiter 77 Cassini 82 Mars Global Surveyor 94 Dawn 203 MESSENGER 236.
Item 16: The type of range data collected 0 No Range Data 1 GSTDN (RE) 6 PLOP or Pseudo-Noise (PRA) 7 PLOP2 (SRA) 8 MU2.
Item 17: The type of range data collected 0 No Angle Data 1 Azimuth/Elevation 2 Hour Angle/Declination 3 X/Y (where +X is East) 4 X/Y (where +X is South).
Item 18: The type of DRVID data collected 0 No DRVID Data 6-8 Same as for Range Type (Item 16).
Item 19: Quality of Doppler measurement.
Item 20: Doppler Bias.
Item 21: Quality of angle measurements.
Item 22: Reference for frequency estimates 0 DCO Level (22 MHz) 1 Sky Level.
Item 23: Simulation Synthesizer Indicator.
Item 24: Receiver Loop Lock Indicator.
Item 25: Transmitter On/Off Indicator.
Item 26: Doppler reference receiver type: 2 MFR 3 Block III 4 Block IV 5 Block V 6 DGT, (arrayed or single station) 7 FSR, arrayed
Item 27: Source designation/exciter type: 1 34-m or 70-m Subnet, Block III/IV Exciter 2 26-m Subnet 3 11-m (OVLBI, Orbiting VLBI) Subnet 4 34-m or 70-m Subnet, Block V Exciter.
Item 28: No process flag and cause: 1 before AOS/after LOS 2 'frozen' Doppler counter 3 illegal reference frequency.
Item 29: Sample Interval in hundredths of a second.
Item 30: High part of Doppler count or downlink phase. To reconstruct double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6 Unit is count.
Item 31: Intermediate part of Doppler count or downlink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 30. Unit is count.
Item 32: Low part of Doppler count or downlink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 30. Unit is count.

Item 33: High part of Range. To reconstruct the double precision value, use the three components below: (HP)*10^8 + (IP)*10^1 + (LP)*10^-6. Unit of the reconstructed value is nanosecond (ns) if Range Type (Item 16) is 1; otherwise, unit is Range-Unit (RU). A Range-Unit is approximately one nanosecond; it is defined as a function of the sky frequency in Hertz (f_sky) and the uplink frequency band: RU(sec) = 0.5*10^-18*f_sky (S-Band uplink) = (11/75)*10^-18*f_sky (HEF X-Band uplink) = (221/1498)*10^-18*f_sky (Block-V Exciter X-Band uplink).
Item 34: Intermediate part of Range. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 33.
Item 35: Low part of Range. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 33.
Item 36: Lowest (last) ranging component.
Item 37: Part 1 of uplink phase. To reconstruct quadruple precision value from four parts, use: (Part 1)*2^40 + (Part 2)*2^16 + (Part 3)*2^-8 + (Part 4)*2^-32 Unit is cycle.
Item 38: Part 2 of uplink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 37.
Item 39: Part 3 of uplink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 37.
Item 40: Part 4 of uplink phase. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 37.

Item 42: Depending on Angle Type (Item 17) the azimuth, hour angle, or Y value for the antenna. Unit is millidegree.

Item 43: If Item 22 is 0, the high part of the Doppler reference frequency (DCO is near 22 MHz). If Item 22 is 1, the sky frequency for the receiver (S-Band near 2 GHz, X-Band near 7 GHz, Ku-Band near 15 GHz, Ka-Band near 32 GHz). The double precision value (in Hertz) can be reconstructed using (HP)*10^3 + (LP)*10^-6.

Item 68: Low part of the ninth high-rate Doppler count or downlink phase measurement. The full double precision variable can be reconstructed using the equation in Item 67. Unit is count.

description: This collection of browse products provides a visual overview of plasma density values and spacecraft trajectories during flybys of Io by Juno while in orbit about Jupiter. Each image consists of two sub-plots. One of which orients the Juno's trajectory in plasma corotational coordinates, the other plots density versus time and provides higher data value resolution. The geometric plasma wake is indicated in both plots. This is merely a cylinder starting at Io and extending in the corotation direction, with the same radius as the moon itself. This is only intended to provide a rough guidline on when wake effects may be present. All plots were generated courtesy of the open-source Matplotlib Python package.

description: This collection contains electron plasma density data along with the key plasma frequencies used to derive these densities from Juno/Waves observations. Data products in this collection are formatted as simple delimited text that should be readable by almost any scientific data analysis package. Within the files are the originally digitized data points along with the resulting characteristic frequencies from cold plasma theory including, but not limited to, the plasma electron frequency, the lower-hybrid resonance, and the upper-hybrid resonance. Electron cyclotron values provided by the Juno FGM instrument team are essential for most calculations. For a full description of the source, usefulness and limitations of data in this collection see the associated documents collection provided in this bundle. Measurements in this small collection were derived from data gathered during one or more flybys of Europa and thus are provided along with plasma corotational coordinates. Since flybys occur infrequency, most of the data in the bundle may be found in the primary Jovicentric collection. All data values were digitized manually using the open-source Autoplot program.

The main body of the New Horizons spacecraft is roughly triangular, and about 0.76m deep, with the tub containing the radioisotope thermoelectric generator extending from the apex. The 2.1m radio dish is attached to the front, flat side of the triangular box. The spacecraft is roughly 2.5 meters across and its mass was 465 kg including propellant at launch. The spacecraft has both spin-stabilized and three-axis stabilized modes, the latter used for science operations. The seven instruments comprising the science payload are mounted on the exterior of the main body.

pds:Field_Binary.pds:description: An ASCII string giving the SFDU Control Authority for this data type. Set to "NJPL", meaning the data description information for this type of SFDU is maintained by the NASA/JPL Control Authority.
An ASCII character giving the SFDU Label Version Identifier. Set to "2", meaning the length given in field 6 is formatted as a binary unsigned integer.
An ASCII character giving the SFDU Class Identifier. Set to "I", meaning this is a Compressed Header Data Object (CHDO) structured SFDU.
These two bytes are not defined.

An ASCII string giving the SFDU Data Description Identifier. Possible values in a TNF are: C123 = Uplink data types C124 = Downlink data types C125 = Derived data types C126 = Interferometric data types C127 = Filtered data types
The number of remaining bytes in the SFDU after the 20-byte SFDU label.

pds:Internal_Reference.pds:comment: Records delivered originally by the DSN were in time order, with records for different TNF data types interleaved. Retaining that structure would have made the PDS label many times larger than the data file itself. To keep the size of the label manageable, the original file was sorted so that all records of a single TNF data type are together. The blocks of homogeneous records were then concatenated -- TNF data type 0, followed by TNF data type 1, ... followed by TNF data type 17. When there were no records of a given TNF data type, that block was omitted. Within each block, the records remain in time order. The label is still long, since each block is a Table_Character with many records containing many fields. But there will never be more than 18 blocks and never more than 18 Table_Character definitions. The document referenced here correctly describes the record formats. Note, however, that the records are no longer in absolute time order. They are in time order within each block and the blocks are ordered by TNF data type.

The MAVEN mission launched on an Atlas V November 18, 2013. After a ten-month ballistic cruise phase, Mars orbit insertion occurred on September 22, 2014. Following a 5-week transition phase, the spacecraft began orbiting Mars at a 75 inclination, with a 4.5 hour period and periapsis altitude of 140-170 km (density corridor of 0.05-0.15 kg/km3). Over a one-Earth-year period, periapsis will precess over a wide range of latitude and local time, while MAVEN obtains detailed measurements of the upper atmosphere, ionosphere, planetary corona, solar wind, interplanetary/Mars magnetic fields, solar EUV and solar energetic particles, thus defining the interactions between the Sun and Mars. MAVEN will explore down to the homopause during a series of five 5-day “deep dip” campaigns for which periapsis will be lowered to an atmospheric density of 2 kg/km3 (~125 km altitude) in order to sample the transition from the collisional lower atmosphere to the collisionless upper atmosphere. These five campaigns will be interspersed though the mission to sample the subsolar region, the dawn and dusk terminators, the anti-solar region, and the north pole.

The OSIRIS-REx spacecraft is a roughly cubic shape, 2.4m x2.4m x3.15m, with two solar panel wings extending from opposite sides. Launch mass including propellant was 1529 kg. Propulsion uses 200 N hydrazine thrusters mounted at the base of the spacecraft. Primary communication is via a 2 meter high gain directional dish antenna. The spacecraft carried a sample return capsule, which was filled at asteroid (101955) Bennu, carried back to Earth by the spacecraft, and delivered to the surface in Septermber 2023. The OSIRIS-REx spacecraft was then redeployed to the asteroid (99942) Apophis for an extended mission to investigate that potentially hazardous body.

A set of very readable web pages connected by hyperlinks that describes the mission of the NASA Deep Space Network and the roles of its many components.

The NASA Deep Space Network (DSN) comprises three Deep Space Communications Complexes (DSCCs) spaced by approximately 120 degrees in longitude and within about 40 degrees latitude of Earth's equator. As the Earth rotates, this configuration provides nearly continuous coverage of spacecraft in the ecliptic -- that is, spacecraft flying to or orbiting most solar system objects. The three DSCCs are as the Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex (GDSCC) near Barstow, California, which is managed by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL); the Canberra Deep Space Communications Complex (CDSCC) in Tidbinbilla, Canberra, Australia, which is managed by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO); and the Madrid Deep Space Communication Complex (MDSCC) in Robledo de Chevala, Spain, which is managed by Instituto Nacional de Tecnica Aeroespacial. Each DSCC includes several Deep Space Stations (DSSs, or antennas), a Signal Processing Center (SPC), and administrative and support facilities. Each DSCC handles several types of data including: frequency and timing, tracking, telemetry, command, monitor, radio science, and very long baseline interferometry. These data types support uplink (to spacecraft) or downlink (from spacecraft) operations or passive reception. Data received from spacecraft are relayed via the local SPC to the Network Operations Control Center (NOCC) at JPL in Pasadena, where they are distributed to the offices responsible for each spacecraft. Commands, generated in those offices, are sent via the NOCC, SPC, and DSS to the spacecraft. The antennas are divided according to aperture size into subnets. For more information, see https://www.nasa.gov/communicating-with-missions/dsn/

An overview of the capabilities available from the Deep Space Network to support flight projects and experiment investigations. The capabilities described are focused on deep space missions, near-Earth missions above Geosynchronous Earth Orbit (GEO), and ground-based observational science. Included are tables summarizing uplink commanding, downlink telemetry, radio frequency, and ground communication capabilities as well as pricing information for mission support. The document is aimed at mission designers working at the proposal stage; it is updated as appropriate.

The sub-systems that comprise the OSIRIS-REx spacecraft are the telecommunications subsystem; the power sub-system; the propulsion sub-system; and the guidance, navigation, control (GNC) sub-system. These sub-systems work together to communicate with the Earth, deliver the spacecraft to the target asteroid, and navigate around the asteroid. The spacecraft hosts a navigation camera system (TAGCAMS), a science camera system (OCAMS), a visible and infrared spectrometer (OVIRS), a thermal emission spectrometer (OTES), and a laser altimeter (OLA). The collection, retrieval, storage and return of the asteroid sample is conducted using the Touch-And-Go Sample Acquisition System (TAGSAM), and the Sample Return Capsule (SRC). The combined spacecraft sub-systems and the hosted complement of instrumentation allows the OSIRIS-REx mission to gather data, collect a sample, and safely return the sample to Earth.
